headline: HOW ZERODHA BUILT A PROFITABLE BROKERAGE WITHOUT VENTURE CAPITAL
post_text: A stock broker that has never taken venture money still reported a net profit of Rs 4,237 crore for FY25. Zerodha, started in 2010, is that broker, and its growth came from its own customers.
thread: A stock broker that has never taken venture money still reported a net profit of Rs 4,237 crore for FY25. Zerodha, started in 2010, is that broker, and its growth came from its own customers.

Zerodha is a discount stock broker run by brothers Nithin and Nikhil Kamath. It charges nothing for equity delivery trades and a flat fee on most other trades. Brokerage is its main income, with smaller amounts from other fees and interest.

Many brokers took a cut on every trade. Zerodha went the other way, using flat-fee pricing instead of high commissions. Its 2015 pricing set delivery trades at zero, and it grew without outside funding.
The model paid off in scale. Revenue reached Rs 9,994.5 crore in FY24, and Zerodha held a 15.8 per cent market share with 7.26 million users. FY25 revenue then fell 11.2 per cent as rules tightened.

headline: HOW SEVEN MUMBAI WOMEN TURNED RS 80 INTO A PAPAD COOPERATIVE WORTH MILLIONS
post_text: Seven women in Mumbai started a papad business in 1959 with a sum of just Rs 80. Their cooperative now reports more than $200 million in sales.
thread: Seven women in Mumbai started a papad business in 1959 with a sum of just Rs 80. Their cooperative now reports more than $200 million in sales.
Lijjat makes papads, masalas, wheat flour, chapatis and detergent, and sells them in India and abroad. It is a cooperative, so each member is a co-owner and profits are shared equally.
Lijjat has no single owner. Women roll papad from home through local branches, and any woman who wants to join can approach one. The papad is kept to one standard, and quality is never compromised.
Open membership and fixed quality kept it growing. It employs more than 43,000 women, runs 82 branches across 17 states, and has never struggled to give work to new members.

headline: HOW AMUL'S FARMER-POOLED CO-OP TURNED MILK INTO A RS 1 LAKH CRORE BRAND
post_text: A dairy brand built by 36 lakh farmers pushed its turnover past Rs 1 lakh crore in FY 2025-26. That was an 11% rise on a Rs 90,000 crore base the year before.
thread: A dairy brand built by 36 lakh farmers pushed its turnover past Rs 1 lakh crore in FY 2025-26. That was an 11% rise on a Rs 90,000 crore base the year before.

Amul runs as three layers. Village societies collect milk, district unions process and test it, and a state federation markets the finished products under the Amul name. It also makes dairy goods for other brands.
Rather than dealing with each farmer one by one, Amul groups small milk producers into village-level societies. Much of the money shoppers pay is sent back to those farmers.
That structure has paid off in numbers. Turnover reached Rs 1 lakh crore in FY 2025-26, and the International Cooperative Alliance has ranked Amul the world's No. 1 cooperative.

headline: HOW MEESHO GREW FROM A WHATSAPP SHOPPING IDEA INTO A LISTED E-COMMERCE COMPANY
post_text: Meesho, founded by Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Barnwal, raised $606 million in its IPO. On its first trading day, its shares rose as much as 46% above the issue price of Rs 111. (1/7)
thread: Meesho, founded by Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Barnwal, raised $606 million in its IPO. On its first trading day, its shares rose as much as 46% above the issue price of Rs 111. (1/7)

Founded in 2015, Meesho started as a WhatsApp-based social commerce app for first-time online shoppers. Its two founders, both IIT Delhi graduates, noticed small shopkeepers selling through WhatsApp groups. It is now Bengaluru-based. (2/7)

Meesho is an online marketplace where small sellers list products for buyers. Its sellers are mostly small merchants, and its buyers are value-conscious shoppers, many in Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns. (3/7)
Meesho mainly earns from logistics fees, advertising and other services, rather than taking a cut of every sale. Its separate Meesho Mall channel does charge commissions on products sold there. (4/7)

In its main marketplace, Meesho charges sellers little or no commission, which sets it apart from many rivals. Its asset-light setup and strong base in non-metro cities are central to its pitch. (5/7)

Losses were its biggest test. Its consolidated net loss was Rs 3,941.70 crore in FY25, and festive-season spending widened losses again to Rs 490.67 crore in the December 2025 quarter. It kept growing, and by the March 2026 quarter the loss had narrowed 88% to Rs 166 crore. (6/7)

In FY26, which ended March 2026, revenue rose about 35% to Rs 12,626 crore and net loss stood at Rs 1,358 crore. Lesson: fast growth with low prices still needs a clear route to profit, so track losses as closely as sales. (7/7)

headline: HOW RAPIDO WENT FROM BIKE TAXI BOOKINGS TO A $3 BILLION RIDE-HAILING COMPANY
post_text: Rapido, founded by Aravind Sanka, Pavan Guntupalli and Rishikesh SR, is a ride-hailing app. Co-founder Pavan Guntupalli was turned down by roughly 75 investors before the company secured funding. (1/7)

The company was started in October 2015 under the earlier name theKarrier, by founders who were IIT and PESU alumni. It began with bike taxi bookings. (2/7)

Rapido earns operating revenue from rides and deliveries. In FY25, delivery was its largest stream at Rs 340 crore. It also charges many drivers a flat fee instead of a cut of every fare.

Losses were the biggest test. The net loss was Rs 675 crore in FY23 and Rs 370 crore in FY24, while revenue rose 46.3% to Rs 648 crore. The subscription shift aimed to improve unit economics.

headline: HOW NYKAA WENT FROM A $2 MILLION BET TO A PROFITABLE BEAUTY RETAILER
post_text: Nykaa started in 2012 with $2 million of its founder's own capital. In the quarter ended September 2026, its net profit was more than three times the year-earlier figure. Here is how it happened. (1/7)
thread: Nykaa started in 2012 with $2 million of its founder's own capital. In the quarter ended September 2026, its net profit was more than three times the year-earlier figure. Here is how it happened. (1/7)

Falguni Nayar spent nearly two decades at Kotak Mahindra Capital, rising to managing director. In 2012 she quit and launched Nykaa from Mumbai, when beauty products were rarely bought online in India. She saw a gap. (2/7)
Raising outside money early meant facing hard questions on margins and customer costs. She did not want to be questioned on assumptions. So she put in $2 million of her own. What did she sell? (3/7)

Nykaa sold beauty and fashion products online, including international brands such as Estee Lauder, Clinique and Bobbi Brown. Its gross margin was 49.7% in Q2FY25. The bigger question was whether the business could make money. (4/7)

Unlike most startups, Nykaa was already profitable before its IPO. It posted a net profit of 618.5 million rupees for the year to March 31, 2021. Then it hit a limit: shoppers wanted to touch products first. (5/7)

Online-only selling kept costs low at first. But customers wanted to try products before buying. In 2015 Nykaa opened its first physical store, in Delhi. The question was how to grow offline without losing its edge. (6/7)

Nykaa's Q2 FY27 net profit was Rs 101 crore, up from about Rs 33 crore a year earlier, on revenue of Rs 3,006 crore. The company that began with $2 million is now listed. Lesson: prove the model with small, measurable steps before asking others to back it. (7/7)

Nykaa sold beauty and fashion products online, including international brands such as Estee Lauder, Clinique and Bobbi Brown. Its gross margin was 49.7% in Q2FY25. The bigger question was whether the business could make money.

Unlike most startups, Nykaa was already profitable before its IPO. It posted a net profit of 618.5 million rupees for the year to March 31, 2021. Then it hit a limit: shoppers wanted to touch products first.

Online-only selling kept costs low at first. But customers wanted to try products before buying. In 2015 Nykaa opened its first physical store, in Delhi. The question was how to grow offline without losing its edge.

headline: HOW DREAM11 PIVOTED TO FREE-TO-PLAY AFTER INDIA BANNED ITS PAID CONTESTS
post_text: Dream11 once earned roughly 95% of its revenue and all of its profit from paid contests. A 2025 law banned those contests. Here is how it happened. (1/7)
thread: Dream11 once earned roughly 95% of its revenue and all of its profit from paid contests. A 2025 law banned those contests. Here is how it happened. (1/7)

Harsh Jain and Bhavit Sheth, childhood friends, started Dream11 in Mumbai in 2008. Jain had first seen fantasy football while studying abroad in 2001. The IPL was growing, and they saw a gap. Their first version did not catch on fast. Why? (2/7)

The first product needed more tweaks. The founders made it far simpler to use than Western fantasy models. In 2012 they launched freemium fantasy cricket, where fans could play free or pay to enter. But how did a free app make money? (3/7)

Fans build virtual teams of real players, and points come from those players' real match performance. Fans pay entry fees for contests with cash prizes, and that is how money came in. Its biggest bet was on one sport. (4/7)
Cricket sat at the core of the product, and its focus on the sport helped grow the user base. Then a new law arrived, changing everything the company had built. (5/7)

In August 2025 Parliament passed a law banning real-money online games. Dream11 halted paid contests on 22 August 2025. It chose not to challenge the law and moved to free-to-play, funded by ads and sponsors. (6/7)

Today Dream Sports, the parent company, is valued at $8 billion. In December 2025 it split into eight units after the ban wiped out 95% of its revenue. Lesson: never let one revenue line carry the whole business. (7/7)
story_text:
Dream11 once earned roughly 95% of its revenue and all of its profit from paid contests. A 2025 law banned those contests. Here is how it happened.

Harsh Jain and Bhavit Sheth, childhood friends, started Dream11 in Mumbai in 2008. Jain had first seen fantasy football while studying abroad in 2001. The IPL was growing, and they saw a gap. Their first version did not catch on fast. Why?

The first product needed more tweaks. The founders made it far simpler to use than Western fantasy models. In 2012 they launched freemium fantasy cricket, where fans could play free or pay to enter. But how did a free app make money?

Fans build virtual teams of real players, and points come from those players' real match performance. Fans pay entry fees for contests with cash prizes, and that is how money came in. Its biggest bet was on one sport.

Cricket sat at the core of the product, and its focus on the sport helped grow the user base. Then a new law arrived, changing everything the company had built.

In August 2025 Parliament passed a law banning real-money online games. Dream11 halted paid contests on 22 August 2025. It chose not to challenge the law and moved to free-to-play, funded by ads and sponsors.

Today Dream Sports, the parent company, is valued at $8 billion. In December 2025 it split into eight units after the ban wiped out 95% of its revenue. Lesson: never let one revenue line carry the whole business.

Groww's app lets users trade stocks and F&O, not just buy mutual funds. Its stock product launched in 2020. Traders pay a flat Rs 20 per executed F&O order, whatever the trade size. Derivatives soon became the biggest earner. (3/7)

Derivatives were the biggest earner. In Q4 FY26, equity derivatives made up 55% of Groww's total revenue. Total revenue reached Rs 1,505 crore, up about 88% from a year earlier. Then regulators stepped in. (4/7)
Groww's flat Rs 20 fee was not new, because Zerodha used flat fees first. Groww's pitch was simpler: a cheap, easy app for first-time investors. Then, in 2024, the rules around F&O changed. (5/7)

In 2024, SEBI raised F&O contract sizes and cut weekly expiries. That directly hit Groww's derivatives income. Groww pushed into margin trading, which was 5% of revenue in Q4 FY26, up from 2% a year earlier. The latest quarterly numbers show where it stands now. (6/7)

Groww had about 1.34 crore active clients in September 2026, a 29.16% share of India's NSE active clients. Its Rs 100 listing and Rs 169 peak came on top of that base. Lesson: serve first-time investors well, and do not let one risky product carry the business. (7/7)

headline: HOW PHYSICSWALLAH WENT FROM A FREE YOUTUBE CHANNEL TO A PROFITABLE EDTECH COMPANY
post_text: PhysicsWallah's profit more than doubled in a year, from Rs 69.7 crore to over Rs 140 crore. It began as a free YouTube physics channel. Here is how it happened. (1/7)
thread: PhysicsWallah's profit more than doubled in a year, from Rs 69.7 crore to over Rs 140 crore. It began as a free YouTube physics channel. Here is how it happened. (1/7)

Alakh Pandey, a physics teacher from Prayagraj, started his YouTube channel in 2016. He saw students who could not afford costly coaching. Free lessons drew crowds, but a channel is not a company. (2/7)

In June 2020, Prateek Maheshwari joined him and they incorporated PhysicsWallah. Maheshwari had built PenPencil, a software tool for coaching institutes. Their first paid course cost just Rs 999. (3/7)

Students and parents pay for online courses, offline classes and books. Online revenue rose 39% to Rs 1,954 crore in FY26, roughly half of all revenue. Offline centres were the next big piece to build. (4/7)
Its courses can start as low as $50 for an entire year. That low price became its central idea. Keeping costs under control was the next test. (5/7)

In Q4 FY25, PhysicsWallah's EBITDA was a loss of Rs 204 crore. A year later, the same quarter showed EBITDA of Rs 65 crore. Paid users, offline growth and tighter costs were behind it. But the next quarter was harder. (6/7)

FY26 revenue rose 35% to Rs 3,900 crore. The September 2026 quarter brought profit above Rs 140 crore, after a Rs 88.3 crore loss in the quarter before. Lesson: find a price your users can pay, then grow only as fast as the business can fund. (7/7)

Alakh Pandey, a physics teacher from Prayagraj, started his YouTube channel in 2016. He saw students who could not afford costly coaching. Free lessons drew crowds, but a channel is not a company.

In June 2020, Prateek Maheshwari joined him and they incorporated PhysicsWallah. Maheshwari had built PenPencil, a software tool for coaching institutes. Their first paid course cost just Rs 999.

Students and parents pay for online courses, offline classes and books. Online revenue rose 39% to Rs 1,954 crore in FY26, roughly half of all revenue. Offline centres were the next big piece to build.

Its courses can start as low as $50 for an entire year. That low price became its central idea. Keeping costs under control was the next test.

In Q4 FY25, PhysicsWallah's EBITDA was a loss of Rs 204 crore. A year later, the same quarter showed EBITDA of Rs 65 crore. Paid users, offline growth and tighter costs were behind it. But the next quarter was harder.

FY26 revenue rose 35% to Rs 3,900 crore. The September 2026 quarter brought profit above Rs 140 crore, after a Rs 88.3 crore loss in the quarter before. Lesson: find a price your users can pay, then grow only as fast as the business can fund.

headline: HOW ZETWERK TURNED A FLOPPED SOFTWARE IDEA INTO A ₹15,913 CR MANUFACTURING NETWORK
post_text: Zetwerk's revenue rose 40.4% in FY26 to ₹15,913 crore. Its net loss widened to ₹1,606 crore in the same year. Here is how it happened. (1/7)
thread: Zetwerk's revenue rose 40.4% in FY26 to ₹15,913 crore. Its net loss widened to ₹1,606 crore in the same year. Here is how it happened. (1/7)

Amrit Pratik Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan both worked in manufacturing sourcing at ITC. They incorporated Zetwerk in Bengaluru in December 2017. Their first product was software to run factories. Factories did not buy it. What came next? (2/7)
The first idea flopped within a few months. Buyers had clearly not taken to it. The founders changed the model instead. What did they build in its place? (3/7)

The new model pools capacity from third-party suppliers and Zetwerk's own plants. Today it serves over 1,000 customers through more than 5,000 suppliers. Clients include Siemens Gamesa and CG Power. How does it earn from this? (4/7)

Zetwerk wins an order, splits it into parts, and hands them to workshops it does not own. It buys in its own name and takes title to the goods. Its FY26 manufacturing EBITDA margin was 6.03%. Why is that margin so thin? (5/7)

Zetwerk calls itself a universal factory. It runs 26 facilities across India, the US, Germany and Spain. It also uses 6,979 third-party suppliers, coordinated through its Zetwerk OS software. Growth has a cost. (6/7)

Today FY26 revenue is ₹15,913 crore, up 40.4%, yet the net loss is ₹1,606 crore. Sales growth shows demand, not profit. Lesson: track cash from day one, because operating cash outflow hit ₹682 crore. (7/7)

headline: HOW EMERGENT WENT FROM A DUNZO CO-FOUNDER'S NEXT STEP TO A $1.5 BILLION VIBE-CODING UNICORN
post_text: Emergent's valuation jumped fivefold in about four months, from $300 million to $1.5 billion. Founded in 2024, it lets anyone build apps by typing plain instructions. Here is how it happened. (1/7)
thread: Emergent's valuation jumped fivefold in about four months, from $300 million to $1.5 billion. Founded in 2024, it lets anyone build apps by typing plain instructions. Here is how it happened. (1/7)

Twin brothers Mukund and Madhav Jha founded Emergent in 2024. Mukund had co-founded grocery delivery startup Dunzo in 2014. They believed access, not ideas, was what stopped people from building software. Their answer was a product built for non-coders. (2/7)

Emergent's AI agents turn a plain-language description into a full working app. Individuals and small businesses use it to build software without hiring engineers. Over 12 million apps have been built on it. Who pays, and how many? (3/7)

Emergent has more than 2 lakh paying customers. It has not shared how many free users convert to paid. Revenue splits roughly one-third US, one-third Europe, and about 9% India. Its pitch to those customers is what sets it apart. (4/7)

Emergent says it is not a coding tool for developers. It calls itself an engineering team in a box. Its agents handle architecture, database, code, testing, bug fixes and deployment. It also built its own coding agent. (5/7)

Dunzo, which Mukund co-founded, shut down after failing to sustain funding. He left Dunzo in 2023. Jha then spent Emergent's first five public days on customer support. Growth brought rivals like Lovable, Cursor and Replit. (6/7)

Today Emergent is valued at $1.5 billion, with $230 million raised across three rounds. That is the fivefold jump from the first post. Lesson: solve access for the people you serve, and keep close to their problems. (7/7)

thread: Fractal Analytics shares listed below their IPO price on February 16, 2026. The issue price was ₹900, but the stock listed at ₹876 on NSE. Here is how it happened. (1/7)

story_text:
Fractal Analytics shares listed below their IPO price on February 16, 2026. The issue price was ₹900, but the stock listed at ₹876 on NSE. Here is how it happened.

In 2000, two IIM Ahmedabad alumni, Srikanth Velamakanni and Pranay Agrawal, started Fractal in Mumbai. Businesses were piling up data but not using it well. Who would pay for a fix?

Fractal sells AI and data analytics to large companies in finance, retail and healthcare. Most of its revenue comes from overseas, mainly the US. How did that become money?

Revenue from operations rose 26% to ₹27.65 billion in the year ended March 2025. The early model was mostly consulting. Later, the firm added its own software platforms to the mix.

In 2006, Fractal answered a P&G search for analytics partners. Srikanth Velamakanni later said that pilot changed the company's fortunes. The bigger test came from inside the company.

Three of the five co-founders left between 2007 and 2012. A board-level split in 2007 pushed the firm to refocus its work. Only Srikanth and Pranay stayed on to lead it.

Fractal's IPO was worth ₹2,834 crore, and its market value after listing was about ₹15,477 crore. After a muted debut at ₹876, the lesson: stick with a hard problem, change the model slowly, and expect a bumpy market debut.

headline: HOW ATHER ENERGY WENT FROM IIT MADRAS SCOOTER DREAM TO A LISTED EV MAKER
post_text: Ather Energy cut its FY25 loss to ₹812 crore from ₹1,059.7 crore. It also listed on the stock exchanges in May 2025. Here is how it happened. (1/7)

story_text:
Ather Energy cut its FY25 loss to ₹812 crore from ₹1,059.7 crore. It also listed on the stock exchanges in May 2025. Here is how it happened.

In 2013, Tarun Mehta and Swapnil Jain, two IIT Madras engineering graduates, started Ather in Bengaluru. They wanted to replace the petrol engine with an electric drive. The first scooter was still years away.

Ather sells electric two-wheelers and smart accessories to riders across India. Software subscriptions and charging add to its income. A scooter still needs power, so charging became the next problem.

Ather built Ather Grid, its own fast-charging network, in 18 cities. It also built AtherStack, its own software platform. Building both took money, and the FY24 net loss was ₹1,059.7 crore.

The fix came through margins. Adjusted gross margins roughly doubled in one year, the company said. It also moved to cheaper lithium iron phosphate batteries. Next came the stock market.

In May 2025, Ather listed on the NSE and BSE after a ₹2,981 crore IPO. Of that, ₹2,626 crore was fresh money for the company. Shares were priced at ₹321 each. So where does it stand now?

Its FY25 loss was ₹812 crore. By FY26, total income reached ₹3,823 crore, up 66%, and volumes hit a record 2,62,942 units. Lesson: fix what makes your product usable, like charging, and track margins as you grow.

Licious once had just 15 days of cash left after a key investor backed out. Here is how the Bengaluru meat startup got there, and how it climbed back.

Vivek Gupta and Abhay Hanjura, two friends who had left stable corporate jobs, started Licious in Bengaluru in 2015. Meat in India was mostly sold by local butchers, often with low hygiene standards. They decided to fix that.

Licious sells fresh chicken, seafood, marinades and eggs to households online. It also sells through quick commerce apps such as Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart. The real question is how the money comes in.

Most of its revenue comes from selling its own meat, seafood and eggs. In FY24, 85% of revenue came through its own platform, not outside partners. Cutting outside channels came at a cost.

Abhay and Vivek refused to outsource anything: sourcing, processing, cold chain or delivery. They started in a 3,000 sq ft unit in Bangalore with just 100 orders a day. They expanded only after reaching 1,000 orders daily. Then cash nearly ran out.

At one point, Licious had just 15 days of cash left when a key investor backed out. The founders paid salaries from their own savings. Their rule was simple: salaries go out on time, no matter what. So how did it recover?

Licious reported FY25 revenue of ₹795 crore, up 16%, and cut its losses by 45%. The company that once had 15 days of cash now plans bigger. Lesson: protect payroll first, and own the parts of your chain that decide quality.

headline: HOW SEEKHO GREW REVENUE 12X IN ONE YEAR WHILE ITS LOSS GREW 8X
post_text: Seekho's revenue grew over 12 times in FY25, to Rs 141.5 crore. Its net loss grew over 8 times too, to Rs 38.8 crore. Here is how it happened. (1/7)
thread: Seekho's revenue grew over 12 times in FY25, to Rs 141.5 crore. Its net loss grew over 8 times too, to Rs 38.8 crore. Here is how it happened. (1/7)

Three IIT Kanpur friends, Rohit Choudhary, Keertay Agarwal and Yash Banwani, started Seekho in 2020. They saw a gap for practical, bite-sized learning in local languages, aimed at people beyond the big metros. (2/7)

Seekho's product is a library of over 10,000 short videos, mostly in Hindi and other Indian languages. Each lesson runs about two to five minutes. Most of its users are in smaller Indian cities and beyond. (3/7)
Paying subscribers bring in most of its revenue. A smaller share comes from ads. The company says more users are now willing to pay for digital content, which is how the subscriptions grew. (4/7)

Seekho says its content is built to uplift viewers, unlike YouTube or Instagram. It calls itself a Netflix for learning, with lessons told as episodic series. Growth needed fuel, and that fuel was costly. (5/7)

The big risk was marketing. In FY25, Seekho spent over Rs 134 crore on advertising and marketing. Its net loss rose from Rs 4.6 crore in FY24 to Rs 38.8 crore, so the company needed fresh money to keep going. (6/7)

In September 2025, Seekho raised $28 million led by Bessemer Venture Partners, at a $180 million valuation. Revenue rose over 12 times, but the loss rose over 8 times. Growth alone does not prove a healthy business. (7/7)

headline: HOW BOMBAY SHAVING COMPANY CUT ITS NET LOSS FROM ₹58 CR TO ₹9 CR AS REVENUE DOUBLED
post_text: Bombay Shaving Company cut its net loss from ₹58 crore to ₹9 crore in FY26, while its revenue rose 139% in the same year. Here is how it happened. (1/7)
thread: Bombay Shaving Company cut its net loss from ₹58 crore to ₹9 crore in FY26, while its revenue rose 139% in the same year. Here is how it happened. (1/7)

Shantanu Deshpande quit McKinsey after five years. In 2016 he co-founded Bombay Shaving Company in Gurugram with Deepu Panicker, Raunak Munot and Rohit Jaiswal. They wanted to improve everyday shaving. Who would pay for that? (2/7)

Its buyers are individual consumers who purchase grooming products online and elsewhere. Bombay Shaving Company and its women's label Bombae brought in ₹581 crore in FY26, over 91% of operating revenue. Where did that growth come from? (3/7)

The company earns mainly by selling its own products. Its services arm, the B2B digital marketing brand 100Days, grew its services revenue to ₹48 crore in FY26. The bigger shift was in where it sold. (4/7)

It did not stay online only. Sales now run through its own website, online marketplaces, quick commerce apps and offline retail. Spreading across channels cost money, so spending became the next test. (5/7)

The biggest risk was the loss. In FY25 the net loss was ₹58.2 crore. The company kept advertising growth far below sales growth, lifting ad spend 55% to ₹158 crore while revenue rose 139%. Did that work? (6/7)

By FY26 the net loss had shrunk to ₹9 crore, and adjusted EBITDA turned positive at ₹2 crore, its first ever. The company targets ₹1,000 crore revenue for FY27. Lesson: grow sales faster than the cost of winning them, and check that gap every quarter. (7/7)

headline: HOW FURLENCO WENT FROM A FURNITURE SALE LOSS TO A ₹59.5 CRORE PROFIT
post_text: Furlenco's net profit jumped nearly 20 times in one year, from ₹3.1 crore in FY25 to ₹59.5 crore in FY26. Here is how a furniture rental idea got there. (1/8)
thread: Furlenco's net profit jumped nearly 20 times in one year, from ₹3.1 crore in FY25 to ₹59.5 crore in FY26. Here is how a furniture rental idea got there. (1/8)

It started in Bengaluru in 2011. Founder Ajith Mohan Karimpana moved from New Jersey and tried to sell furniture he had bought less than two years earlier. He got back only about 10% of its value. Why should owning furniture hurt this much? (2/8)

Furlenco rents furniture and appliances on a monthly subscription, not a one-time sale. Its catalogue has more than 300 SKUs across 28 cities. Rentals made up about 92% of FY26 operating revenue. How does that become money? (3/8)

Customers pay a monthly rent for each item. In FY26, operating revenue rose 61.9% to ₹370.4 crore. Rental income alone was ₹341.1 crore, while furniture sales brought in ₹29.4 crore. The model is capital-intensive, so cash is always tight. What did it do differently? (4/8)

It set up its own furniture manufacturing plant to control cost and quality. A 2017 YourStory report said few furniture rental firms ran their own design and manufacturing units. Its hardest test came next. What happened? (5/8)

The pandemic hit. Demand for rental furniture held up, but Furlenco was starved for cash. Sheela Foam, which owns Kurlon and Sleepwell mattresses, invested in 2023, committing ₹300 crore for a 35% stake. Did that fix the business? (6/8)

Furlenco's FY26 net profit of ₹59.5 crore was up from ₹3.1 crore, and it was in the red until FY24. Lesson: survive the cash crunch first, then chase scale. A ₹1,000-1,200 crore IPO is reportedly planned. (7/8)

headline: HOW APPLIED COMPUTE REACHED A $100M RUN RATE IN 18 MONTHS BEFORE A $4.5B DEAL
post_text: Applied Compute reached a $100 million annual revenue run rate less than 18 months after founding. Then Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy it for $4.5 billion. Here is how it happened. (1/7)
thread: Applied Compute reached a $100 million annual revenue run rate less than 18 months after founding. Then Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy it for $4.5 billion. Here is how it happened. (1/7)

Three former OpenAI researchers started Applied Compute: Yash Patil, Rhythm Garg and Linden Li. Based in San Francisco, they believed a company's AI should be specific to that company and owned by it. Here is what they built. (2/7)

Applied Compute trains custom AI models for enterprise customers, often on open-source foundations. It then runs those models on its own cloud. Companies like Microsoft, Shopify, DoorDash and Harvey use it. How does it differ? (3/7)

headline: HOW OFBUSINESS TURNED 73 REJECTED PITCHES INTO A ₹724 CRORE PROFIT
post_text: OfBusiness's funding pitch was turned down 73 times in just six months. Its FY26 profit reached ₹724 crore. Here is how it happened. (1/7)
thread: OfBusiness's funding pitch was turned down 73 times in just six months. Its FY26 profit reached ₹724 crore. Here is how it happened. (1/7)

Trading brings in most of the revenue, but lending brings in most of the profit. Its lending arm Oxyzo finances small businesses. In FY26 the financial services segment earned ₹505 crore before tax, nearly 55% of group segment profit. (4/7)

After 73 rejections, FY26 profit rose 21% to ₹724 crore from ₹597 crore, while revenue fell 7% to ₹20,645 crore. Lesson: check that every sale makes money before you chase size. (7/7)

headline: HOW MILKY MIST WENT FROM ERODE MILK TRADING TO A RS 3,138 CRORE DAIRY BRAND
post_text: Milky Mist started as a milk trader in Erode in 1985. In FY26 it reported Rs 3,138 crore in revenue. Here is how a milk trading family got there. (1/7)
thread: Milky Mist started as a milk trader in Erode in 1985. In FY26 it reported Rs 3,138 crore in revenue. Here is how a milk trading family got there. (1/7)

T. Sathish Kumar's family already traded milk when the business began in Erode, Tamil Nadu, in 1985. He joined in, then noticed that milk supply was largely unorganised. What would he build from that? (2/7)

Milky Mist makes packaged dairy such as paneer, cheese, curd, ghee, butter, ice cream and yogurt. Everyday shoppers buy these off store shelves. Nearly 60% of FY26 revenue came from paneer, cheese and curd. Where does the margin come from? (3/7)
These categories are generally more profitable than plain milk. Its operating margins stayed around 12-14% in recent years. The next move changed the business itself. (4/7)
In 1994 it began making paneer. It launched the Milky Mist brand in 1997. Over three decades it grew to more than 400 products. But one weakness was still hiding in its supply chain. (5/7)

About 94.51% of its raw milk came from Tamil Nadu in FY26, and 69.23% of revenue came from its home market. Its answer was to build its own factories, cold chains and distribution over nearly four decades. Did it pay off? (6/7)

FY26 revenue reached Rs 3,138.36 crore, up 33.6% from Rs 2,349.50 crore, and net profit hit Rs 127 crore. The milk trader from 1985 now sells more than 400 products. Lesson: know your raw material deeply, then add value on top of it. (7/7)

These categories are generally more profitable than plain milk. Its operating margins stayed around 12-14% in recent years. The next move changed the business itself.

In 1994 it began making paneer. It launched the Milky Mist brand in 1997. Over three decades it grew to more than 400 products. But one weakness was still hiding in its supply chain.

post_text: Zepto's revenue more than doubled to ₹22,624 crore in FY26, yet the company lost ₹5,905 crore that same year. Here is how it happened. (1/7)
thread: Zepto's revenue more than doubled to ₹22,624 crore in FY26, yet the company lost ₹5,905 crore that same year. Here is how it happened. (1/7)

Aadit Palicha and Kaivalya Vohra started Zepto in 2021 in Mumbai. During the pandemic, getting groceries could take days. Their first try, KiranaKart, was hard to scale. So what did they do next? (2/7)
